attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you flip the Player sprite’s image assets horizontally and give them descriptive names?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might the walkBear and swimBear image assets be used in the project?

❓ What does the flip horizontal tool do in the paint editor? Why might it be useful?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can duplicate an asset by clicking on it, then selecting Duplicate from the left side menu. Once duplicated, remind the ninja to open the new asset to edit it, then revise its name.

💡 The flip horizontal tool flips an image horizontally, creating left facing versions of the existing right facing image assets. This is useful when a sprite faces a variety of directions in the project.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by creating multiple Player sprite image assets to be used throughout the project!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images, tiles, and tilemap stored in My Assets. Find the walkBearRight and swimBearRight image assets.


Duplicate the walkBearRight and swimBearRight image assets, then edit the new assets. Use the flip horizontal tool in the top left of the paint editor, to create a left facing version of both images. Give the new assets descriptive names: walkBearLeft and swimBearLeft.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type assets, a dot operator, and the asset type, followed by the name of the asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to display a tilemap on screen?

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap be typed in the setCurrentTilemap function?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to check the documentation if they need help displaying a tilemap on screen.
steps.instructions:
Set a tilemap to appear on screen!

 

Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // game initialization comment at the top. Display the tilemap saved in My Assets underneath.

 

Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you edit the vx and vy parameters of the moveSprite function so the Player sprite can only move horizontally?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which function should be used to place the Player sprite on a specific tile on the tilemap?

❓ What should the vx and vy parameters of the moveSprite function be set to so the Player sprite can only move horizontally?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the vx parameter sets how quickly the sprite moves left and right, and the vy parameter sets how quickly the sprite moves up and down.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance placing the Player sprite, setting it to move with direction buttons, or setting the camera to follow it.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!

 

Under // game initialization, add code to create a Player sprite. Name the sprite bearSprite, set its image image to the walkBearRight image asset, and place the sprite on the left side of the tilemap.

 

Set the Player sprite to move around the tilemap with direction buttons. Since this is a 2D platformer project, the Player sprite should only be able to move horizontally (right and left) on the tilemap.

 

Then, set the Player sprite to stay in screen, and set the camera to follow the Player sprite.

 

Click ▶ to test the Player sprite’s movement.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the acceleration (ay) and velocity (vy) code in the correct places in your program?
steps.senseiHelp:
﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the Player sprite’s y-acceleration need to be set in a 2D platformer tilemap?

❓ Why should the Player sprite’s y-velocity be set to a negative value when the A button is pressed?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In a 2D platformer tilemap, “gravity” is needed to simulate real world events. In order to jump up onto a platform, the Player sprite’s y-velocity needs to be set to a negative value. A positive y-acceleration value will cause the Player sprite to fall back down to the ground, when it steps off a platform. The values can be changed to increase or decrease the speed at which the Player sprite jumps up and falls back down.
steps.instructions:
Make the Player sprite jump when the A button is pressed!

 

Under the Player sprite code, use the Player sprite name and a dot operator to set its y-acceleration (ay) to 500 to “pull” the Player sprite down to the ground, like gravity.

 

Then, add a // game events comment and an A button pressed event to make the Player sprite jump, using the Player sprite name and a dot operator to set its y-velocity (vy) value to -200.

 

Click ▶ to test the Player sprite’s jumping mechanics.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the direction parameter in the isHittingTile function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the Player sprite only be able to jump when standing on a wall tile?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Allowing the Player sprite to only be able to jump when standing on a wall tile simulates real world events. By not being able to jump while in midair, it adds an additional challenge for the user playing the game.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite jumps while in midair!

Allow the Player sprite to jump only if it is standing on the ground.

 

Add an if conditional inside the A button press event. Open Scene and drag [is (sprite) hitting wall (direction)] inside the parentheses of the if conditional. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 


mySprite.isHittingTile(Collision

Direction.Left)


The isHittingTile function takes 1 parameter: direction. Update the sprite name and select .Bottom for the Collision Direction using the dot operator.

 

Cut and paste the Player sprite’s y-velocity (vy) code inside the if conditional.

 

Click ▶ to test that the Player sprite is only able to jump when touching a tilemap wall tile.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the tile parameter in each onOverlapTile event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you match the tile asset to the state of the swimming variable in each onOverlapTile event?

❓ What else might happen when the Player sprite overlaps a skyTile or swimTile?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has correctly matched the tile asset to the state of the swimming variable in each onOverlapTile event. Prompt them to consider if the Player sprite has overlapped a skyTile, would they be swimming or not swimming (and vice versa for the swimTile).

💡 In this project, the swimming variable will be used to control several game conditions. When the Player sprite overlaps each type of tile, the sprite’s properties will be set to showcase which area of the tilemap it’s in.
steps.instructions:
Create a Boolean variable that can be toggled to show whether the Player sprite is swimming or not swimming.

 

Under // game initialization, declare a swimming variable, set to false.

 

Open Scene and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (tile) at (location)] under // game events.

 

Set the tile parameter to the swimTile tile asset. Set the swimming variable to true inside the onOverlapTile event.

 

Create another onOverlapTile event, with the tile parameter set to the skyTile tile asset. Set the swimming variable to false inside this onOverlapTile event.

 

Now, the swimming variable will change when the Player sprite overlaps a swimTile or skyTile, which will be used to change other things in the code later on.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a Boolean OR operator || to check if one of two conditions are true?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the code in the condition check to see whether the Player sprite can jump or swim upwards?

❓ What condition(s) need to be true in order for the Player sprite’s y-velocity to change by -200?



Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the logic of the condition with the ninja. If the Player sprite is swimming, meaning the swimming variable is true, the Player sprite will be able to “swim” upwards underwater. OR, if the Player sprite is on land and the bottom of the Player sprite is touching a wall tile, then it can jump. Only one of the 2 conditions needs to be true in order for the code to run.
steps.instructions:
Allow the Player sprite to swim underwater!


Inside the parentheses of the if conditional in the A button press event, use a Boolean OR operator followed by the swimming variable to allow the Player sprite to continually “swim” upwards when the A button is pressed.


Click ▶ to test that the Player sprite can swim in the water and jump on the land.

steps.hints: ❓Did you declare a Boolean parameter by typing the parameter name, then a colon : and the parameter type boolean?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to change the sprite’s image when it’s facing different directions in a 2D platformer project?

❓ How do you set a Boolean function parameter?

❓ When should the Player sprite’s image be set to the walkBearRight image asset? When should it be set to the walkBearLeft image asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that in a 2D platformer project, the user’s perspective is from the side. This means that instead of looking down from the top, the user should be able to see the sprite’s profile from whichever direction they are facing. As a result, in order to make the game more lifelike, the Player sprite’s image should match the direction that it’s facing.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for assistance in adding a Boolean parameter to the function. Point out how using a descriptive parameter name such as isFacingRight can be helpful in determining what code the function runs.

💡 If the isFacingRight parameter is true when the function is called, the Player sprite’s image will be set to the walkBearRight image asset. If the isFacingRight parameter is false when the function is called, the Player sprite’s image will be set to the walkBearLeft image asset
steps.instructions:
Change the Player sprite’s image when it moves in different directions!


Define a spriteImage function with an isFacingRight Boolean parameter. 


Add an if conditional inside that checks if isFacingRight is true, then sets the sprite image to the walkBearRight image asset. 


Add an else if condition that checks if isFacingRight is not true, using a Boolean NOT operator, then sets the sprite image to the walkBearLeft image asset.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use 2 onEvent controller functions to change the facingRight variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to make something happen whenever the left or right buttons are pressed?

❓ Why should the facingRight variable be passed to the spriteImage function as the Boolean parameter?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for assistance in adding the 2 controller events. Make sure they’ve created an event for when both the left and right direction buttons are pressed.

💡 Have the ninja notice how the value of the facingRight variable changes when different direction buttons are pressed. Using a Boolean variable can help better keep track of game conditions throughout a project. In this example, the variable is keeping track of the direction that the Player sprite is facing, which is then passed to the spriteImage function to correctly set the Player sprite’s image.
steps.instructions:
Change the Player sprite’s image when the left and right direction buttons are pressed!


Under // game initialization, declare a facingRight variable, set to true.


Under // game events, set facingRight to true whenever the right button is pressed. Set facingRight to false whenever the left button is pressed.


Add an onUpdate event under // game events. Call the spriteImage function inside the onUpdate event using facingRight as the argument.


Click ▶ to test out the image code.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a Boolean AND operator && in the if and else if conditions to check if !isSwimming?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the Boolean AND operator used to check for multiple conditions in the spriteImage function?

❓ Why is it useful to use the Boolean NOT operator to check for a false condition? 

❓ Why does the spriteImage function call need to be updated?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The if condition checks if the Player sprite isFacingRight AND not swimming. If so, the sprite’s image will be set to the walkBearRight image asset. The else if condition checks if both the isFacingRight AND swimming variables are false, meaning the Player sprite is on land and facing left. If so, the sprite’s image will be set to the walkBearRight image asset. 

💡 The Boolean NOT operator evaluates the opposite of the variable value. This is another way of checking if a variable is false and can reduce the amount of code needed. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use the documentation for assistance in adding a second Boolean parameter to the function. Point out that the project will throw an error if only 1 argument is passed, instead of 2, in the function call.
steps.instructions:
Check if the Player sprite is swimming in the spriteImage function.


In the spriteImage function definition, create a second Boolean parameter: isSwimming.


Inside both the if and else if conditions, type a Boolean AND operator then check that isSwimming is not true using a Boolean NOT operator.


Inside the onUpdate event, update the spriteImage function call using the swimming variable as an argument for the isSwimming parameter.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create 2 more else if conditions that check for the isFacingRight AND isSwimming parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ When will the Player sprite be “swimming”?

❓ Why do 2 additional else if conditions need to be added to the spriteImage function definition?

❓ When will the Player sprite’s image be set to the swimBearRight and swimBearLeft image assets?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that once the Player sprite overlaps a swimTile on the tilemap, the swimming variable will be set to true, which will be passed to the spriteImage function when it is called. Prompt the ninja to open the tilemap and notice where the swimTile assets are located on the tilemap.

💡 Encourage the ninja to think through the logic of the conditional in the spriteImage function definition. Because 2 parameters are used and there are 4 possible sprite images, each of the 4 unique variable condition combinations need to be checked for.

💡The third else if condition checks if the Player sprite isFacingRight AND swimming. If so, the sprite’s image will be set to the swimBearRight image asset. The fourth else if condition checks if the isFacingRight variable is false AND if the Player sprite is swimming. If so, the sprite’s image will be set to the swimBearLeft image asset.
steps.instructions:
Change the Player sprite image when it moves in different directions under water!


In the spriteImage function definition, add 2 more else if conditions. If isFacingRight AND isSwimming are both true, then set the Player sprite image to the swimBearRight image asset. 


Then, if isFacingRight is not true AND isSwimming is true, set the Player sprite image to the swimBearLeft image asset.

Click ▶ to see the Player sprite image change as it moves left and right on the ground and  underwater.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the randint function to randomly select a row for the Food sprite to appear on?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might a Food sprite be placed on the tilemap?

❓ What does the DestroyOnWall sprite flag do? Why might it be used?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the randint function to randomly select a row for the Food sprite to appear on. Encourage the ninja to open the tilemap asset in My Assets to identify which rows contain water tiles.

💡 The DestroyOnWall sprite flag will destroy the given sprite when it collides with a wall tile. In this example, the Food sprite will “swim” from right to left across the tilemap. Because it will have this sprite flag turned on, it will automatically be destroyed once it reaches the other side of the tilemap. 

💡 Remind the ninja that they should delete .AutoDestroy, then retype the dot operator to update the sprite flag.
steps.instructions:
Create Food sprites for the Player sprite to collect in the water!


Define a makeSalmon function under // game initialization.


Create a sprite using the salmonImage image asset from My Assets and the Food sprite kind. Place each Food sprite on a random water tile on column 19 of the tilemap. 


Set the Food sprites’ x-velocity (vx) to a random negative value so that the sprites move right to left across the tilemap at different speeds. 


Set the Food sprites to destroy on wall. Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) (SpriteFlag.AutoDestroy) (on)] underneath the vx code. Update the sprite name, then change the flag parameter to SpriteFlag.DestroyOnWall and the on parameter to true.

steps.hints: ❓Did you adjust the onUpdateInterval period parameter to change how frequently the Food sprites spawn to make them easier or more difficult to catch?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How frequently might the makeSalmon function be called? How does this change the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to play with the period parameter in the onUpdateInterval function, then notice how that affects how many Food sprites appear on the screen at once. Prompt the ninja to notice that the Food sprites appear at different heights, due to their random row placement.
steps.instructions:
Call the function to create Food sprites!


Use an onUpdateInterval function under // game events to call the makeSalmon function inside the function. Tinker with the period parameter to change how frequently the Food sprites are spawned.


Under the Player sprite code, use the Player sprite name and a dot operator to set the z-property value to 3 to ensure the Player sprite appears in front of the Food sprites.


Click ▶ to test the Food sprite function code.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the allOfKind function to check the length of the array of Food sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does a while loop do? Why might it be used?

❓ What code should be placed inside of the while loop, so that it runs while there are fewer than 6 Food sprites on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡A while loop runs while a certain condition is true. It can be useful for making something happen continuously in a project. 

💡 Remind the ninja that when using a while loop, it’s imperative that the loop has a clear exit condition, otherwise it will throw errors in the project. In this example, once there are 5 Food sprites on the screen, the while loop will stop running.

💡Remind the ninja to check for the length of the array of Food sprites in the while loop condition.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! There are too many Food sprites on the screen. 


Open Loops and drag [while] inside the onUpdateInterval function. Add code inside the parentheses of the while loop to check if the length of the array of Food sprites is less than 6. 


Cut and paste the makeSalmon function call inside the while loop.


Now, the makeSalmon function will only be called while there are fewer than 6 Food sprites on the screen.


Click ▶ to test how many Food sprites appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the salmonCount by 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to increase the salmonCount variable by 1?

❓ What might the salmonCount variable be used for?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that an increment operator can be used to increase the value of a variable by 1.

💡 Point out to the ninjas that variables are useful for collecting and storing information throughout a project. This is a good alternative to showing a score or life variable, and can be used to share information with the user.
steps.instructions:
Count the number of Food sprites the Player sprite overlaps!


Declare a salmonCount variable set to 0 under // game initialization. 


Create an onOverlap event with the Player and Food sprite kinds under // game events. 


Whenever the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite, destroy the Food sprite, then increase the salmonCount by 1.


Click ▶ to test out the overlap code.

steps.hints: ❓Did you find the functions to start and end a screen effect, then use documentation to update the effect properties and parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many seconds might the Player sprite be able to stay underwater for?

❓ How can you change the effect in the functions that start and stop a screen effect?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Explain to the ninja that the endScreenEffect function is very similar to the startScreenEffect function. The endScreenEffect function stops the current screen effect from displaying on the screen. The ninja can delete .blizzard, then retype the dot operator to select a different effect.
steps.instructions:
Add a timer that counts down how long the Player sprite can stay underwater!


Find the 2 onOverlapTile events under // game events. Inside the swimTile onOverlapTile event, add a startCountdown function and update the duration parameter to be the number of seconds the Player sprite can be underwater. 


Inside the skyTile onOverlapTile event, add a stopCountdown function that will reset the timer when the Player sprite comes up for air.


Add the bubbles screen effect to the project, starting the effect when the Player sprite overlaps the swimTile and ending it when the Player sprite overlaps the skyTile.


Click ▶ to test that the countdown timer starts and stops as the Player sprite enters and exits the water.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use + to concatenate the salmonCount variable with a string in the splash function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to concatenate a string with the salmonCount variable in the splash function?

❓ When will a splash screen be displayed on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance concatenating a string with the salmonCount variable in the splash function.

💡 If the Player sprite stays underwater for too long and the countdown reaches 0, a splash screen will be displayed and the game will end. Remind the ninja that a countdown timer is one way to make the project more engaging for the user, creating an extra challenge.
steps.instructions:
Show the user how many Food sprites they caught at the end of the game!


Use an onCountdownEnd function to display a splash screen once the time runs out. Concatenate the salmonCount variable with a string to tell the user how many Food sprites they collected.


End the game after the splash screen is shown.


Click ▶ to see a splash screen appear whenever the timer runs out.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the same values for the 3 variables in the startGame function definition that are used in the variable declarations?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does it mean to initialize a game?

❓ What values will each of the variables be set to when the startGame function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja has already practiced initialization in many ways. Setting variables to a specific value at the beginning of the project creates a starting point that can be updated later. In this example, the variables are declared outside of the startGame function, but their values are set inside the function. This allows the game to be replayed, without the user having to start completely over and read the directions each time.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to initialize the game!


Under // game initialization, define a startGame function.


Inside the function definition, set the initial, or starting values of the facingRight, swimming and salmonCount variables (in that order) using the same values used while the Player sprite is on land.


Cut and paste the code that places the Player sprite on a tile at the top left of the tilemap into the startGame function definition. 


Then, add a // game start comment, and call the startGame function underneath.


Click ▶ to test out the startGame function.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an if/else conditional to give users 2 possible choices at the end of the game?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the ask function similar and different to the askForString and askForNumber functions?

❓ What options does the user have when the countdown ends?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ask function asks the user a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ question. Unlike the askForString function, which asks for a string value, or the askForNumber function, which asks for a number value, the user responds to the ask function with a Boolean value, by pressing the A or B button.
steps.instructions:
Give users a choice to restart the game when the game ends!


Inside the onCountdownEnd event, add an if conditional after the splash screen code. Open Game and drag [ask (title)] inside the parentheses of the if conditional. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.ask(null)

The ask function takes 2 parameters: a title and a subtitle. Update the title with a question that asks the user if they want to play again. 


Inside the condition, call the startGame function.


Add an else condition. Cut and paste the game.over function inside.


Click ▶ to test the choices at the end of the game!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the marquee tool to select and resize the cursor image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might be used for the dialog frame?

❓ How can an image be resized in the paint editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:


💡 Encourage the ninja to use the marquee tool in the paint editor to resize the cursor image.
steps.instructions:
Add instructions to the beginning of the project!


Below // game start, set the dialog frame and dialog cursor above the startGame function call. 


Create and modify 2 new image assets in My Assets: one to be used for the dialog frame, and a duplicated, larger version of the bear image to be used for the dialog cursor. Give both assets a descriptive name, then call the assets in the setDialogFrame and setDialogCursor functions.


Then, create a dialog box to share instructions for the project with the user.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses physics to change how a sprite moves around a 2D platformer tilemap.

validationItems.text: Display a tilemap asset on screen.
Create a Player sprite, set it to stay in screen, and set the camera to follow it.
Use a Boolean OR operator to set the Player sprite’s physics so that it jumps up while standing on the ground and swims while underwater when the A button is pressed.
Use 2 variables with Boolean values to set the different states a sprite might be in.
Use a spriteImage function with nested if/else if conditionals and Boolean operators to change the Player sprite’s image based on the direction it is facing and whether it is on land or underwater.
Use a makeSalmon function to create Food sprites that move across the screen and destroy when they hit a wall.
Call the makeSalmon function inside an onUpdateInterval loop while there are fewer than 6 sprites on a screen.
Start and stop a countdown timer when the Player sprite moves into and out of the water tiles.
Use a startGame function to initialize the game. Call the function at the start of the project and if the user decides to play again.
Provide 2 possible choices at the game end.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using physics and Boolean values to control game conditions in 2D platform tilemap projects. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Taking Control
badges.description: Control the way sprites move and appear on screen in a 2D tilemap project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Gravity of the Situation
badges.description: Use physics to control a sprite’s velocity and acceleration in a 2D tilemap project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Checkin’ it Twice
badges.description: Check for a specific tile image at a specific tilemap location.

badges.title: While You’re At It…
badges.description: Use a while loop to make something happen while a certain condition is true.

badges.title: And the Winner Is…
badges.description: Create a function that uses Boolean operators and values to determine which sprite image to use.

badges.title: Well-Rounded Character
badges.description: Edit an image asset to create multiple versions of an image that faces different directions.
